title: The Day of the LORD Against Babylon
sum: Isaiah's oracles against the nations open with Babylon. The LORD musters an army on a bare mountain, 'from the edge of the sky', and the day of the LORD arrives with terror like labor pains and darkness in the heavens. Then the army is named: the Medes, who cannot be bought off with silver. Babylon, the beauty of the kingdoms, will end like Sodom and Gomorrah, an empty ruin where no Arab pitches a tent and only owls, ostriches and hyenas live.

The chapter moves between a single city and the whole world. It begins with a war against Babylon, widens into cosmic judgment on 'the world' and 'the arrogant', and narrows again to the ruins. Its images return in Jesus' teaching on the end (Matthew 24:29) and in Revelation's Babylon (Revelation 18:2).
readings: Read as history

The oracle looks to the capture of Babylon by Cyrus, king of the Medes and Persians, in 539 BC, and to the slow decline that left it deserted by the early centuries AD. The details of total ruin were not fulfilled at once: Cyrus took the city without a battle, and it remained inhabited for centuries. Readers in this line speak of a prophecy fulfilled over a long span.
Read as a pattern

The day of the LORD against Babylon is a model of God's judgment on every proud empire. The cosmic language (sun, moon and stars) is the prophets' way of saying that a world order is ending, as in Ezekiel 32:7–8. This is how Jesus and Revelation reuse it.
Read as still to come

Some futurist readers hold that the total ruin of Isaiah 13:19–22 has never happened, and expect a rebuilt Babylon, or the world system called Babylon in Revelation 17–18, to be destroyed at the end of the age.

views.H: Babylon was a great city in Isaiah's century but not yet an empire; it was ruled by Assyria and kept revolting. The Medes were a growing power on the Iranian plateau. In 539 BC Cyrus took Babylon, and later rulers (Xerxes, Alexander, the Seleucids) moved power elsewhere. Strabo, in the time of Augustus, describes much of the city as deserted.
views.C: Most critical scholars date chapter 13 to the 500s BC, when the Medes and Persians threatened Babylon, and think it was placed at the head of the collection by later editors. Others (Erlandsson) argue that an Assyrian-period date fits, since the Medes were already known and Babylon was destroyed by Sennacherib in 689 BC.
views.J: Rashi and Radak read the chapter of the fall of Babylon to Darius the Mede and Cyrus, the end of the exile.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in the darkened sun and moon a picture of the end of the age that Jesus took up (Matthew 24:29), and in Babylon a type of the world opposed to God (Revelation 17–18). Jerome and Calvin read it historically of the Medes and Persians, while noting its use in the New Testament.
views.F: Some dispensational writers hold that Babylon must be rebuilt and destroyed again, because Isaiah 13:20 says it will never be lived in. Others reply that Babylon's long abandonment already fulfills the verse.

deep.b: For Isaiah 13–23 the Plain is translated from the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), the basis of modern Hebrew Bibles. The Dead Sea Scrolls were consulted for every verse through the transcriptions of Martin Abegg, James Bowley and Edward Cook (ETCBC dss): the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, complete for these chapters), 1QIsa-b (1Q8), and the Cave 4 fragments 4QIsa-a (4Q55), 4QIsa-b (4Q56), 4QIsa-c (4Q57), 4QIsa-e (4Q59), 4QIsa-f (4Q60) and 4QIsa-o (4Q68). The Greek was read in Swete's edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus. Readings of Ziegler's critical Greek text, of Symmachus, of the Targum (in Chilton's translation) and of the Latin Vulgate are given as reported by those editions and the commentaries cited. The variants cover the main places where the witnesses differ in meaning and name the witnesses on each side; spelling differences, very common in the Great Isaiah Scroll, are not listed. The Plain leaves the Leningrad Codex in three places: 14:4 ('the onslaught', where the scrolls themselves are split), 16:4 and 17:11 (other vowels; at 16:4 with the Greek) and 19:18 ('City of the Sun', with two Qumran scrolls).

In Isaiah's own day Assyria was the great enemy, yet the collection begins with Babylon (13:1–14:23) and returns to it (21:1–10). Scholars suggest several reasons. Editors living after 586 BC, when Babylon had destroyed Jerusalem, may have placed it first as the greatest oppressor. Babylon also stood for pride against God from Genesis 11 on, so it makes a fitting head of the list. The oracle on Assyria (14:24–27) follows immediately, and the two together frame the collection: every empire, Assyrian or Babylonian, falls under the LORD's plan 'drawn up for all the earth' (14:26).

The cosmic language of 13:9–13, a darkened sky and a shaken earth, is typical of 'the day of the LORD' (Joel 2:10; Joel 2:31; Amos 5:18–20). Jesus uses 13:10 in his teaching on the end of the age (Matthew 24:29), and Revelation's sixth seal and fall of Babylon draw on the whole chapter.

echoes: Genesis 11:1–9; Genesis 19:24–25; Jeremiah 50:1–51:64; Joel 2:10; Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:24–25; Revelation 6:12–14; Revelation 18:2

settings.by: Isaiah, speaking for the LORD of Armies
settings.to: Judah (or, on the exilic dating, the exiles in Babylon), about Babylon
settings.when: Debated: Isaiah's own century, when Babylon rebelled against Assyria, or the years before 539 BC
settings.why: To assure God's people that the empire that seemed unbeatable was under God's sentence. The oracle is not addressed to Babylon for its own sake; it tells Judah that no empire, however splendid, outlasts the LORD's plan, and so it calls them to trust God rather than fear or court the great powers.
settings.readers: For exiles in Babylon after 586 BC the oracle became a promise of release.
views: Erlandsson and others: Isaiah addressed Judah about Babylon's revolts against Assyria, and the oracle was later read of 539 BC.
Most critical scholars: a prophet in the 500s BC announced the coming of the Medes against Babylon.

title: How You Have Fallen, Shining One
sum: Chapter 14 opens with mercy: the LORD will choose Israel again and bring it home, with foreigners joining it. Then the freed people sing a taunt over the king of Babylon. The earth rests, the cedars of Lebanon celebrate, and Sheol stirs to greet the tyrant, whose bed is now maggots. 'How you have fallen from the heavens, Shining One, son of Dawn!' He planned to climb above the stars of God, and he is thrown out unburied.

Three shorter oracles follow. The LORD swears to break Assyria 'in my own land' (14:24–27). In the year King Ahaz died, Philistia is warned not to celebrate the death of its oppressor, because a worse one is coming; and the envoys of the nations are told that the LORD has founded Zion as a refuge for the poor (14:28–32).
readings: Read as satire on a king

The taunt is political satire. A tyrant who called himself divine is mocked with the language of a myth about a star-god who tried to climb too high. The point is that human pride, however high it climbs, ends in the grave.
Read as the fall of Satan

From Tertullian and Origen on, many Christian readers saw in 14:12–15 the fall of the devil, whose pride ('I will make myself the Most High's equal') turned an angel of light into God's enemy. Many still read it so, often as a double reference: the king, and the power behind him.
Read with its myth

The poem draws on Canaanite stories: Helel son of Shachar ('Dawn'), the Mount of Meeting in the heights of Zaphon, and the god Athtar who could not fill Baal's throne. Isaiah uses a story his hearers knew to show that the LORD alone is Most High.

views.H: No single king of Babylon is named. Proposals include Sargon II, who died in battle in 705 BC and was not buried, Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar and Nabonidus. Sargon also held Babylon's throne, which fits 'king of Babylon'. The Philistia oracle is dated to the year Ahaz died, about 715 BC (or 727 BC on another chronology).
views.C: Critics note that 14:1–4a and 14:22–23 link an older taunt to Babylon, and many think the taunt was first composed about an Assyrian king (Ginsberg: Sargon) and later reapplied. The Canaanite parallels (Ugarit's Athtar; KTU 1.23 on Shachar) are widely accepted.
views.J: The Talmud reads the boast of 14:13–14 of Nebuchadnezzar, and the rabbis note the reply: the heavens are far above him (Bavli Chagigah 13a; Bavli Pesahim 94a–b). Jewish interpreters read the chapter of the king, not of a fallen angel.
views.X: Tertullian (Against Marcion 5.11, 5.17) and Origen (On First Principles 1.5.5) read 14:12 of Satan, and Jerome's Latin lucifer became the devil's name. Calvin rejected this reading as ignorant of the context. Many modern Christians hold both: the passage speaks of the king, and shows the pattern of satanic pride.
views.F: Some futurist interpreters see in the king of Babylon a type of the future Antichrist, whose fall will be like this tyrant's.

deep.h: Helel, Lucifer and the morning star
deep.b:
The word helel occurs only here. It comes from the root halal, 'to shine', and most read it as the morning star, the planet Venus, which rises brightest just before dawn and fades as the sun comes up: a perfect picture of a glory that vanishes. The Greek translated heosphoros, 'dawn-bringer', and Jerome's Latin lucifer, 'light-bearer', both ordinary words for the morning star. The KJV kept the Latin as a name, 'Lucifer, son of the morning', and so the word became a name of the devil in English.

The identification with Satan came through reading Isaiah 14 with Luke 10:18, where Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven, and with Ezekiel 28:12–19. But the same star image is used of Christ: in Revelation 22:16 Jesus calls himself 'the bright Morning Star', and 2 Peter 1:19 speaks of the morning star rising in believers' hearts. A star can be a symbol of glory rightly given or of glory grasped.

echoes: Genesis 11:4; Ezekiel 28:1–19; Ezekiel 31:1–18; Ezekiel 32:17–32; Psalm 48:2; Psalm 82:6–7; Daniel 4:30–33; Luke 10:15; Luke 10:18; Revelation 12:7–10

settings.by: Isaiah, or a later voice in the Isaiah tradition
settings.to: Israel in exile or under foreign rule
settings.when: Linking the Babylon oracle to the taunt
settings.why: To set Babylon's fall inside God's purpose for Israel: the LORD will choose Israel again, bring it home and let foreigners join it. The fall of the empire matters because it frees God's people.
views: Traditional readers and some scholars: Isaiah foresaw the return and wrote these verses with the oracle.
Most critical scholars: an editor of the exilic period added the verses to tie the Babylon oracle to the hope of chapters 40–55.

settings.what: The taunt over the king of Babylon
settings.by: The freed people, as the prophet gives them the words
settings.to: The dead king of Babylon, but for Israel's ears
settings.when: Imagined on 'the day the LORD gives you rest'
settings.why: A taunt song (mashal) mocks a fallen tyrant. For an oppressed people, singing it in advance was an act of faith: the king who seemed divine would end as a corpse. The heavenly language exposes his real sin, pride that wanted God's place.
views: Ginsberg and others: the taunt first mocked Sargon II, who died unburied in 705 BC, and was later applied to Babylon.
Others: it was composed for the fall of the Babylonian empire in the 500s BC.

settings.by: The LORD of Armies, through Isaiah
settings.to: Judah, under Assyrian domination
settings.when: Isaiah's ministry, probably before 701 BC
settings.why: To promise that the LORD would break Assyria on his own mountains and lift its yoke. The oracle is the key to the whole collection: 'This is the plan drawn up for all the earth.'

settings.to: Philistia, and envoys of the nations; heard in Judah
settings.when: The year King Ahaz died (about 715 BC, or 727 BC)
settings.why: The Philistines hoped the death of an oppressor would free them, and sent envoys to Jerusalem, perhaps to win Judah into a revolt. Isaiah warns that worse is coming, and gives the envoys Judah's answer: Zion's security lies in the LORD, not in alliances.
views: Most scholars: an Assyrian king (Tiglath-pileser III, died 727 BC, or Shalmaneser V, 722 BC) has died, and a worse one will follow.
Others, including Jewish interpreters: Ahaz has died, and Hezekiah, who struck Philistia (2 Kings 18:8), will be the adder.

title: A Night of Ruin in Moab
sum: The oracle concerning Moab begins with a single night of destruction: Ar and Kir, Moab's chief cities, are ravaged and silenced. Then the poem tours the country as its people mourn, climbing to their high places, shaving heads and beards, putting on sackcloth and howling from the rooftops. Refugees flee south to Zoar with what they can carry, across the Wadi of the Poplars, and the waters of Dimon run with blood.

Most striking is the prophet's own grief: 'My heart cries out for Moab.' The lament is for an old enemy of Israel, and much of it is reused in Jeremiah 48. Whether Isaiah mourns in earnest or in irony, the chapter shows a prophet who feels the suffering of another nation.
readings: Read as a real lament
The prophet weeps for Moab because God's judgment, even on enemies, is a terrible thing. This is the plain sense of 15:5 and 16:9–11, and most readers take it this way.
Read as a mock lament
Some scholars (Brian Jones and others) read the poem as irony: Judah's prophet imitates a funeral song in order to celebrate Moab's fall, as a taunt.
Read as an old poem reapplied

The note in 16:13–14 says this was 'the word the LORD spoke long ago' and gives it a new deadline. Many think Isaiah took up an older lament over Moab, perhaps from the 800s BC, and applied it to his own day.

views.H: Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. The places named run from the Arnon gorge north to Heshbon and south to Zoar. Assyrian records show Moab paying tribute to Tiglath-pileser III and Sennacherib; it suffered attacks from Arab tribes and later from Babylon (582 BC, according to Josephus). Which invasion is meant is unknown.
views.C: Hitzig (1831) argued that the poem is older than Isaiah, perhaps by Jonah son of Amittai. Many scholars accept that 15:1–16:12 is older material and 16:13–14 Isaiah's update. The close parallel with Jeremiah 48 shows how prophetic poems were reused.
views.J: The midrash contrasts Israel's prophets, who wept over the nations ('My heart cries out for Moab'), with Balaam, who tried to curse a whole people (Numbers Rabbah 20:1).
views.X: Christian readers have found here a picture of God's compassion even in judgment, and of the prophet's sympathy as a model for preaching. Calvin notes that the prophet's tears show that God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23).
views.F: Some futurist readers apply the oracles on Moab, Edom and Ammon to modern Jordan, expecting a future fulfillment; most interpreters see them fulfilled in antiquity, when Moab disappeared as a people.

deep.b:
Jeremiah's oracle on Moab reuses much of Isaiah's, sometimes word for word and sometimes rearranged. The site follows Isaiah's wording, and Jeremiah 48 will be translated to match it wherever the Hebrew is the same.

IsaiahJeremiah
Isaiah 15:2–3 (shaved heads, sackcloth, rooftops)Jeremiah 48:37–38
Isaiah 15:4–6 (Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz; Zoar; Nimrim)Jeremiah 48:34
Isaiah 15:5 (the climb to Luhith; the Horonaim road)Jeremiah 48:5
Isaiah 16:6 (Moab's pride)Jeremiah 48:29–30
Isaiah 16:7 (Kir-hareseth)Jeremiah 48:31
Isaiah 16:8–10 (the vine of Sibmah; the harvest shout)Jeremiah 48:32–33
Isaiah 16:11 (the prophet's grief like a harp)Jeremiah 48:36
Isaiah 16:12 (the high place)Jeremiah 48:35

Two more parallels are close: Isaiah 15:2 (Dibon) and Jeremiah 48:18, 22; Isaiah 15:7 (the riches they made) and Jeremiah 48:36; Isaiah 16:2 (the fords of the Arnon) and Jeremiah 48:20. Outside chapters 15–16, Isaiah 24:17–18 ('terror, pit and trap', part 24-30) is repeated almost word for word in Jeremiah 48:43–44. Jeremiah also uses other sources: Jeremiah 48:45–46 draws on the old song of Numbers 21:28–29 and the oracle of Balaam (Numbers 24:17). Jeremiah also ends with a promise that Isaiah lacks: the LORD will turn Moab's fortunes around at the end of days (Jeremiah 48:47).

echoes: Numbers 21:26–30; Numbers 24:17; Deuteronomy 2:9; 2 Kings 3:4–27; Jeremiah 48:1–47; Ezekiel 25:8–11; Amos 2:1–3; Zephaniah 2:8–11

settings.by: Isaiah, possibly taking up an older lament
settings.to: Judah, about Moab, Judah's neighbor and old rival
settings.when: Unknown; perhaps an Assyrian or Arab invasion of Moab in Isaiah's century
settings.why: The lament teaches Judah that the LORD's judgment reaches its neighbors, and invites compassion rather than gloating. In the middle (16:1–5) Moab is pictured seeking refuge in Zion, which tells Judah what Zion is for: a shelter under a just Davidic king. Moab's pride shuts it out.
views: Most interpreters: the prophet truly mourns.
Jones and others: the lament is ironic and celebrates Moab's fall.

title: Moab Seeks Shelter in Zion
sum: Moab's refugees, huddled at the fords of the Arnon, are told to send tribute to the ruler of Judah and to ask for shelter. A voice pleads, 'Shelter the people driven out', and the answer looks ahead to a throne made firm by loyal love in David's tent, with a judge who seeks justice. But Moab's pride, named four times over, stands in the way.

The lament resumes over Moab's famous vineyards, the vine of Sibmah whose runners reached the desert and the sea. The prophet weeps with Jazer, his inner self throbbing like a harp. A prose note closes the oracle: what was spoken long ago will now happen within three years, counted exactly.
readings: Read as politics
Moab, threatened from the south or east, might seek protection from Judah. Isaiah uses that possibility to describe what a just Davidic throne should be, a refuge for the oppressed.
Read as messianic hope
The throne 'in David's tent' with a judge who 'looks for justice' (16:5) has been read by the Targum and by Christian interpreters as the Messiah's kingdom, which welcomes outsiders.
Read as an old oracle updated
The note in 16:13–14 shows how prophecy was reused: an older word about Moab receives a new, specific deadline from Isaiah.

views.H: The 'three years' of 16:14 may point to Sargon's campaigns about 715–711 BC or Sennacherib's in 701 BC, when Moab paid tribute to Assyria. Sela (16:1), 'rock', may be the place in Edom, or simply a rocky stronghold.
views.C: 16:13–14 is often taken as Isaiah's own addition to an older poem, and 16:4b–5 as a later insertion that brings a Davidic hope into the lament. Others think the hope belongs to Isaiah's theology of Zion.
views.J: The Targum reads 16:1 as Moab bringing tribute 'to the Messiah of Israel', and 16:5 of the throne of the Messiah.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in 16:5 the reign of Christ, whose throne is established in loyal love (Luke 1:32–33), and in Moab's plea the welcome of the nations. Ruth the Moabite in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:5) is often recalled.
views.F: Some futurist readers apply the shelter of Moab's outcasts to the protection of Israel's remnant in Jordan during a future tribulation; others find this a modern reading foreign to the text.

echoes: Ruth 1:1–4:22; 2 Kings 3:4; Psalm 61:3–4; Isaiah 9:6–7; Isaiah 11:1–5; Jeremiah 48:29–38; Amos 9:11; Luke 1:32–33

settings.what: Moab's plea to Zion and the Davidic answer
settings.by: The prophet, giving words to Moab's refugees and the answer from Zion
settings.to: Judah's king and people, with Moab's envoys pictured at the gate
settings.when: Within the Moab oracle; the setting is a Moabite appeal for refuge
settings.why: To show what Zion is for: a shelter for the oppressed under a just king of David's line. Moab is told to send tribute and ask asylum, and the answer is a throne made firm by loyal love. The plea fails only because of Moab's pride (16:6).
views: Some: Moab did seek Judah's protection during an invasion.
Others: the prophet imagines the plea to make his point about Zion.

settings.to: Judah
settings.when: Isaiah's ministry; perhaps about 715 BC
settings.why: To apply an older oracle to the present: within three years, counted as exactly as a hired worker counts his time, Moab's glory will be humbled. For Judah, the precise date was a test of the prophet's word; some suggest it also warned against relying on Moab as an ally, though the text does not say so.

title: Damascus Falls, and Jacob's Glory Fades
sum: The oracle concerning Damascus announces that Aram's capital will become a pile of rubble, and that Ephraim, its partner in war against Judah, will share its fate. Israel's glory will shrink like a body wasting away, like a field after the harvest, like an olive tree with only a few olives left at the top. On that day people will look to their Maker instead of the altars and Asherah poles they made.

Israel planted delightful gardens but forgot the Rock where it could shelter. The chapter ends with a different scene: nations roar like the sea against God's people, but at his rebuke they flee like chaff, gone before morning.
readings: Read as history
The oracle belongs to the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 734–732 BC (Isaiah 7–8). Tiglath-pileser III took Damascus in 732 BC, and Samaria fell in 722 BC.
Read as a call to turn
The center of the chapter is 17:7–8: people will look to the Holy One of Israel. Judgment strips away false supports so that people return to their Maker.
Read as still to come

Some modern prophecy teachers say Damascus has never 'ceased to be a city' and expect its destruction in a future war. Others answer that the oracle was fulfilled when Aram's kingdom ended in 732 BC; the city was later rebuilt, as many ruined cities were.

views.H: Damascus fell to Tiglath-pileser III in 732 BC; he deported its people to Kir and executed King Rezin (2 Kings 16:9). Assyrian records list the deportation of Aram's people. Ephraim lost Galilee and Gilead at the same time and Samaria fell ten years later.
views.C: 17:1–6 is widely accepted as Isaiah's own from 734–732 BC. 17:7–8 and 17:9–11 may be later expansions; 17:12–14 is a separate piece, often linked with Sennacherib's retreat in 701 BC (Isaiah 37:36).
views.J: Rashi reads the nations of 17:12–14 as Sennacherib's army, which was struck by night, and 'gone by morning' as the morning after (2 Kings 19:35).
views.X: Christian interpreters read 17:7 as the turning of people to God when their idols fail, and 17:12–14 as a picture of God's protection of his people against the hostile world (compare Psalm 46).
views.F: Futurist readers often cite 17:1 as an unfulfilled prophecy of the destruction of modern Damascus; many other interpreters regard it as fulfilled.

echoes: 2 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 16:5–9; Isaiah 7:1–9; Isaiah 8:4; Amos 1:3–5; Psalm 46:2–7; Psalm 2:1–4; Jeremiah 49:23–27

settings.to: Judah, about Damascus and Ephraim
settings.when: About 734–732 BC, during the Syro-Ephraimite war
settings.why: Aram and Ephraim had attacked Judah to force it into an anti-Assyrian alliance (Isaiah 7:1–9). Isaiah tells Judah not to fear them: both will be stripped bare. Only a few olives will be left.

settings.to: Israel (Ephraim), and Judah reading after it
settings.when: After the judgment of 17:1–6
settings.why: To name the real cause of the disaster: Israel forgot the God who rescues and turned to altars, Asherah poles and fast-growing gardens. Judgment aims to turn people back to the Holy One of Israel.

settings.to: Judah
settings.when: Perhaps the Assyrian threat of 701 BC
settings.why: To comfort Judah: armies roar like the sea, but God rebukes them, and they vanish overnight. 'That is the share of those who strip us.'

title: Envoys from Beyond the Rivers of Cush
sum: Woe to the land of buzzing wings beyond the rivers of Cush. Its envoys come down the Nile in papyrus boats, a tall and smooth-skinned people, feared far and wide. The prophet sends the messengers home with a word for the whole world: watch for the signal on the mountains. The LORD will wait, still as summer heat, and then prune the nations like a vine before harvest.
The chapter ends with a reversal: the same tall people will bring gifts to the LORD of Armies at Mount Zion. A nation that came to make an alliance will come to worship.
readings: Read as diplomacy
About 715–701 BC the Kushite kings of Egypt sent envoys to rally the small states of the Levant against Assyria. Isaiah tells Judah to send them back: the LORD, not Cush, will decide the outcome.
Read as world mission
The ending (18:7) pictures a distant African people coming to worship the God of Israel. Christian readers connect it with the Ethiopian official of Acts 8 and with Psalm 68:31.

views.H: The 25th Dynasty, kings from Cush (Nubia), ruled Egypt from about 728 to 656 BC. Their envoys sought allies against Assyria. Tirhakah, a Kushite king, marched against Sennacherib in 701 BC (Isaiah 37:9).
views.C: 18:1–6 is generally accepted as Isaiah's own; 18:7, in prose, is often thought a later addition that draws on the language of 18:2 and the hope of the nations' pilgrimage to Zion (2:2–4).
views.J: Rashi and Radak relate 18:7 to the end of days, when the nations will bring Israel's exiles home as an offering to the LORD (compare 66:20).
views.X: The Ethiopian official baptized by Philip (Acts 8:26–39), reading Isaiah, has long been seen as a first fulfillment of 18:7 and Psalm 68:31. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church has treasured these verses.
views.F: Some read 18:7 of a future gathering of the nations to Jerusalem in the messianic age.

echoes: Isaiah 20:3–5; Isaiah 37:9; Isaiah 45:14; Psalm 68:31; Zephaniah 3:10; Acts 8:26–39

settings.what: Woe to the land beyond the rivers of Cush
settings.to: Envoys from Cush in Jerusalem, and Judah's leaders
settings.when: About 715–701 BC, when Kushite Egypt sought allies against Assyria
settings.why: To tell Judah not to join the Kushite alliance: the LORD is watching quietly and will act in his own time. The ending turns the envoys' mission around: the people who came seeking allies will one day come with gifts for the LORD.

title: Blessed Is My People Egypt
sum: The LORD rides a fast cloud into Egypt, and its idols shake. Egypt turns on itself, its spirit drains away, and a hard master rules it. The Nile dries up, and with it the fishing, the flax and the weaving. The famous sages of Zoan and Memphis give foolish advice, and the LORD mixes a spirit of confusion into them until Egypt staggers like a drunk.

Then the chapter turns, in five 'on that day' sayings. Egypt fears Judah; five towns speak Hebrew; an altar to the LORD stands in Egypt; the Egyptians cry out and the LORD sends a savior and heals them; and a highway joins Egypt and Assyria in worship. The LORD blesses all three: 'Blessed is my people Egypt, and the work of my hands, Assyria, and my inheritance, Israel!'
readings: Read as judgment and politics
The poem (19:1–15) describes Egypt's weakness in Isaiah's time, divided and then conquered. Its point for Judah is simple: do not rely on Egypt.
Read as the conversion of the nations

The prose (19:16–25) moves from fear to worship. Egypt and Assyria, Israel's two oppressors, are named God's people. Christian and Jewish readers alike see here one of the Bible's widest visions of the nations' inclusion.
Read as a story about the dispersion
The Greek reads 19:25 as 'my people who are in Egypt and among the Assyrians', the Jewish communities abroad. On this reading the prophecy is about Jews in Egypt and their worship there.

views.H: Egypt was divided under rival dynasties until the Kushite Piye and Shabaka conquered it (about 728–716 BC). Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671 BC. Jewish settlers later lived at Elephantine (with a temple, destroyed 410 BC) and in Alexandria; Onias IV built a temple at Leontopolis about 160 BC, citing this chapter (Josephus).
views.C: Most critical scholars date the poem (19:1–15) to Isaiah and the prose (19:16–25) to later centuries, perhaps the Persian or Hellenistic period, when Jews lived in Egypt. The 'City of the Sun' variant may reflect debate about the temple at Leontopolis.
views.J: The Mishnah (Menachot 13:10) treats the temple of Onias as legitimate in a limited sense, which the Talmud connects with this chapter (Bavli Menachot 109b–110a). The Targum makes the three blessings of 19:25 all Israel's.
views.X: Christian interpreters from Eusebius and Jerome on saw here the gospel's spread to Egypt and the church of Alexandria. The Coptic Orthodox Church honors 19:1 in its tradition of the Holy Family's flight into Egypt, when idols are said to have fallen at Jesus' coming.
views.F: Many futurist readers see the highway and the united worship of Egypt, Assyria and Israel as a picture of the coming messianic kingdom.

deep.b:
The prose half of the chapter moves step by step. First, Egypt fears Judah and the LORD's plan (19:16–17). Second, five towns speak 'the language of Canaan' and swear by the LORD (19:18). Third, an altar and a standing stone for the LORD stand in Egypt as a witness, and when Egypt cries out, the LORD sends a savior (19:19–22). Fourth, a highway runs from Egypt to Assyria, and they worship together (19:23). Fifth, Israel stands with them as 'a blessing at the center of the world' (19:24–25).

The movement goes from terror to worship, and from Israel's special status to a blessing shared. The vocabulary is Exodus vocabulary: cry, oppressors, savior, strike, heal, know the LORD. The nation that once enslaved Israel is to be rescued by Israel's God, just as Israel was. This is why many readers count 19:24–25 among the high points of the Old Testament's hope for the nations, beside Genesis 12:3 and Isaiah 2:2–4.

echoes: Exodus 7:5; Exodus 12:12; Exodus 14:4; Judges 3:9; Jeremiah 46:13–26; Ezekiel 29:1–30:26; Zephaniah 3:9; Zechariah 14:18–19; Ephesians 2:14–19

settings.to: Judah, about Egypt, the ally Judah's leaders courted
settings.when: Isaiah's ministry, probably about 715–701 BC
settings.why: To show Judah that Egypt was no refuge: its gods, its river and its wise men would all fail. The poem prepares for Isaiah's warnings against the Egyptian alliance (30:1–7; 31:1–3).

settings.by: The prophet, or later voices in the Isaiah tradition
settings.to: Judah, and later Jewish communities in Egypt
settings.when: Debated: Isaiah's lifetime, or the Persian or Hellenistic period
settings.why: To announce that the LORD's purpose for Egypt and Assyria is not only judgment but healing and worship. For Jews living in Egypt the passage gave a way to see their life abroad within God's plan, and for all readers it widens God's people beyond Israel.
views: Oswalt and others: the passage belongs to Isaiah's vision of the nations (2:2–4).
Most critical scholars: written in the Persian or Hellenistic period, perhaps by Jews in Egypt.

title: Isaiah Walks Barefoot
sum: In the year Sargon's field marshal took Ashdod, the LORD told Isaiah to take off his sackcloth and sandals. For three years he went about stripped and barefoot as a sign. Then the LORD explained: this is how the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and Cush, young and old, to their shame.

The people of the coast, who had looked to Egypt and Cush for rescue, will be left asking, 'And us? How will we get away?' The chapter is the only prose narrative in the oracles against the nations, and the only extended sign-act Isaiah performs.
readings: Read as a sign-act
Prophets often acted out their message (Jeremiah 13; Ezekiel 4–5). Isaiah's appearance as a captive was a living warning, and the three years kept it before the public.
Read as a political warning
The real audience is Judah's court, tempted to join Ashdod and Egypt against Assyria. The sign tells them what will become of that alliance.

views.H: Sargon's inscriptions describe the revolt of Ashdod (about 713–711 BC), its appeal to Egypt and to neighbors including Judah, and the flight of its usurper Iamani to the border of Cush, whose king handed him over in chains. The 'Tartan' was Assyria's field marshal (2 Kings 18:17).
views.C: The chapter is widely accepted as an authentic report about Isaiah, written in the third person. Its date, about 711 BC, is one of the firmest in the book.
views.J: Ibn Ezra and Maimonides (Guide 2.46) held that the act took place in prophetic vision, since a prophet would not go naked in public. Other Jewish interpreters understood him to have removed only his outer garment.
views.X: Christian interpreters have seen in Isaiah a prophet willing to be humiliated for his message, and some compare the sign to Christ, who was stripped (Matthew 27:28, 35).
views.F: Futurist readers do not usually treat this chapter as unfulfilled; it is read as fulfilled under Assyria.

echoes: 2 Kings 18:17; 1 Samuel 19:24; Micah 1:8; Jeremiah 13:1–11; Jeremiah 27:2; Ezekiel 4:1–5:4; Isaiah 30:1–7; Isaiah 36:6

settings.by: The LORD, through Isaiah's actions, reported in the third person
settings.to: Judah and its neighbors on the Philistine coast
settings.when: About 713–711 BC, during and after Ashdod's revolt against Sargon II
settings.why: To persuade Judah not to join Ashdod's revolt or trust Egypt and Cush. Isaiah's body showed the end of that hope: the allies would be led off naked. Judah apparently stayed out of this revolt, though it joined the next one in 705–701 BC.

title: Watchman, What of the Night?
sum: Three short, mysterious oracles. The first, 'concerning the wilderness of the sea', is a vision so hard that the prophet is doubled over: a feast, a call to arms, a watchman posted to look for riders. At last the cry comes, 'Fallen! Fallen is Babylon!', and its idols lie smashed. The prophet reports it to his threshed people.

The second is two verses long: someone calls from Seir, 'Watchman, how far gone is the night?', and the watchman gives a riddling answer. The third tells the caravans of Dedan and the people of Tema to feed refugees fleeing the sword, and gives Kedar's glory one more year.
readings: Read as visions

The chapter shows the prophet's experience: the shock of a vision (21:3–4), the patient watching (21:8), and the unclear answer (21:12). Prophecy is portrayed as waiting and seeing, not only speaking.
Read as history
Babylon fell in 539 BC to Cyrus with Elamite and Median forces; the Arab oases were attacked by Assyrian and Babylonian kings. The oracles read as messages to Judah about its neighbors' fates.
Read as hope in the night
Jewish and Christian readers have heard 21:11–12 as the question of every waiting people: how long until the morning of God's rescue?

views.H: If the first oracle refers to 539 BC, the feast matches the reports of Herodotus and Xenophon that Babylon fell during a festival (compare Daniel 5). If it refers to the 700s, it may concern Sargon's capture of Babylon (710 BC) or Sennacherib's (689 BC). Dumah, Dedan and Tema were oases on the Arabian caravan routes.
views.C: Many date 21:1–10 to the 540s BC, with the rest of the Babylon material. Others (Erlandsson; Macintosh, Isaiah xxi: A Palimpsest) argue for the Assyrian period. The Aramaic forms in 21:11–12 and the riddle titles suggest a deliberate collection of short pieces.
views.J: The Jerusalem Talmud (Taanit 1:1) reads 21:11 as Israel asking God when the exile under 'Seir' (Rome) will end; the answer is that redemption comes when Israel repents.
views.X: Revelation takes up 21:9 for Babylon the Great (Revelation 14:8; 18:2). John Bowring's hymn 'Watchman, Tell Us of the Night' (1825) made 21:11 an Advent text.
views.F: Some futurist readers apply 'Fallen is Babylon' to a final fall of an end-time Babylon, as in Revelation 18.

echoes: Jeremiah 50:2; Jeremiah 51:8; Daniel 5:1–31; Habakkuk 2:1–3; Revelation 14:8; Revelation 18:2; Genesis 25:13–15; Psalm 130:6

settings.what: The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea
settings.to: His 'threshed' people (21:10), Judah or the exiles
settings.when: Debated: 710 or 689 BC, or before 539 BC
settings.why: To report the fall of Babylon to a people crushed by empires. If Babylon was Judah's hoped-for ally against Assyria, the news was a blow; if Babylon was the oppressor, it was good news. Either way, the prophet's task is to watch and report faithfully.
views: Erlandsson and others: the fall of Babylon to Assyria dashed Judah's hopes in an anti-Assyrian ally.
Most interpreters: the fall to Cyrus in 539 BC.

settings.to: Someone calling from Seir (Edom), and Judah overhearing
settings.when: Unknown; perhaps during Assyrian pressure on Edom and Arabia
settings.why: To answer an anxious neighbor honestly: relief may come, but so may another night. The call to 'turn around and come again' leaves the door open.

settings.to: Judah, about the Arab tribes and oases
settings.when: Probably during an Assyrian campaign in north Arabia, about 715 BC or later
settings.why: To call the oases to show hospitality to refugees and to announce that Kedar's power will end within a year. The precise deadline, like 16:14, made the word testable.

title: The Valley of Vision and the Key of David
sum: The one oracle in the collection against Jerusalem calls it 'the Valley of Vision'. The city is partying on its rooftops, but the prophet weeps for 'my dear people': its leaders ran and were captured, the enemy's chariots filled its valleys. Jerusalem looked to its armory, its walls and its water, but not to the God who planned it all. When the LORD called for mourning, they feasted: 'Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!'

The second half turns on two officials. Shebna, the steward 'over the palace', has cut himself a grand tomb; the LORD will roll him up like a ball and throw him away. Eliakim will receive his robe, his authority and 'the key of David's house'. But even the firm peg will one day give way.
readings: Read as history
The chapter belongs to Hezekiah's reign and the Assyrian crisis, probably 701 BC. The waterworks and wall-building match the archaeology of Jerusalem, and Shebna and Eliakim appear in Isaiah 36–37.
Read as a word on trust
The center is 22:11: 'you never looked to the one who did all this.' Engineering and celebrations are condemned when they replace turning to God.
Read with the New Testament
The key of David passes to Christ (Revelation 3:7), and the steward's office has shaped Christian debate about the keys given to Peter (Matthew 16:19).

views.H: Hezekiah's tunnel and the Broad Wall in Jerusalem date to the late 700s BC. A tomb inscription in Silwan names an official '...yahu, who is over the house', perhaps Shebna. In 701 BC Eliakim was over the palace and Shebna was secretary (36:3).
views.C: Most scholars date 22:1–14 to 701 BC, after Sennacherib's withdrawal; some see in 22:1–4 later images of 586 BC. 22:24–25 is often thought a later addition reflecting Eliakim's fall.
views.J: Rashi reads 22:15–25 of Shebna, whom rabbinic tradition (Bavli Sanhedrin 26a) made a traitor who plotted to hand Jerusalem to Sennacherib. Bavli Yoma 86a draws from 22:14 that some sins are atoned only by death.
views.X: Revelation 3:7 calls Christ the one 'who holds the key of David'. Catholic teaching connects the steward's office with Peter's keys; Protestant and Orthodox teachers read the keys differently (see Christian traditions). Paul quotes 22:13 in 1 Corinthians 15:32.
views.F: Some futurist readers see in Eliakim a type of the Messiah who will rule David's house in the coming kingdom.

deep.b: Across the Kidron valley from the City of David, the village of Silwan sits on a slope cut with rock tombs from the time of the kings of Judah. In 1870 Charles Clermont-Ganneau found an inscription carved over the door of one of them and had it removed to the British Museum. It was too worn to read until Nahman Avigad published it in 1953. It reads, in part: 'This is [the tomb of] ...yahu, who is over the house. There is no silver or gold here, only [his bones] and the bones of his maid-servant with him. Cursed be the man who opens this.' The name is broken off. Avigad and many after him suggested Shebanyahu, the full form of 'Shebna'. The title matches 22:15, and the tomb, high in the rock face, matches 'a man who hews his grave on a height'. The identification cannot be proved, but the inscription shows exactly the kind of monument Isaiah condemned, and the curse on intruders makes the prophet's word, that Shebna would never lie in it, all the sharper.

echoes: 2 Kings 18:18; 2 Kings 18:37; 2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:2–5; 2 Chronicles 32:30; Isaiah 36:3; Matthew 16:19; Revelation 3:7; 1 Corinthians 15:32

settings.what: The oracle concerning the Valley of Vision
settings.to: The people and leaders of Jerusalem
settings.when: Most likely 701 BC, as the city celebrated after the Assyrian army withdrew
settings.why: To shatter a false relief. The city celebrated its escape though its countryside lay in ruins and its leaders had fled; it had prepared for siege without turning to God. Isaiah calls for the mourning they refused, and pronounces their guilt.
views: Others: the crisis of 711 BC, or a picture shaped by 586 BC.

settings.what: Against Shebna; the call of Eliakim
settings.by: The Lord GOD of Armies, through Isaiah
settings.to: Shebna, the palace chief, in person; and the court
settings.when: Hezekiah's reign, before 701 BC
settings.why: To bring down an official who used his power to build his own monument, and to give the office to one who would be 'a father' to Jerusalem. The closing verses warn that even a good official can be dragged down by family and favorites.
settings.readers: For later readers the key of David became an image of rightful authority under God, which the New Testament gives to Christ.

traditions.q: Isaiah 22:22 gives Eliakim 'the key of David's house', and Jesus gives Peter 'the keys of the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 16:19). Do the keys mean an office handed on, like the steward's, and who holds them today?
views: The keys are the authority to govern the house of God, the Church, given to Peter and continued in the bishop of Rome (Catechism 553, 881). Catholic writers such as Stephen Ray argue from Isaiah 22 that the steward of the king's house held an office passed from one holder to the next, and the Lectionary reads Isaiah 22:19–23 with Matthew 16:13–20. Some Protestant scholars also see Isaiah 22 behind Matthew 16:19 (Albright and Mann).

The keys were given to Peter as representative of all the apostles (Matthew 18:18; John 20:23), and every bishop shares them. Peter is honored as first among the apostles, but no single see holds the keys over the others.
The keys are an office and power given by Christ to the whole church to bind and loose sins, exercised above all in absolution and in excluding the openly unrepentant (Smalcald Articles III.7).
The keys are the preaching of the gospel and church discipline, by which the kingdom of heaven is opened to believers and shut to unbelievers (Heidelberg Catechism, questions 83–85).
Christ has given authority to each local congregation to order its worship and discipline its members; no officer holds the keys over the churches (Second London Confession, chapter 26).

title: Howl, Ships of Tarshish
sum: The collection ends with Tyre, the great sea-trading city of Phoenicia. Ships returning from Cyprus hear the news that their home port is gone. Sidon is told to blush: the sea itself laments like a childless mother. Who planned this against the city that handed out crowns? The LORD of Armies, to bring down the pride of all splendor.

Then comes a surprising epilogue in prose. Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, then return to trade like an old prostitute singing for customers. But her profits will be holy to the LORD, food and clothing for those who live in his presence.
readings: Read as history

Tyre was besieged by Shalmaneser V, humbled by Sennacherib (its king fled to Cyprus in 701 BC), besieged by Nebuchadnezzar for thirteen years and taken by Alexander in 332 BC. The oracle may have been reread through these events.
Read as a word against wealth and pride

Tyre stands for commercial power, whose merchants were princes. Revelation 18 takes up the picture for Babylon the Great. Wealth is not condemned in itself, but pride in it is, and in the end it is turned to God's service.
Read as hope for the nations

The ending (23:17–18) does not destroy Tyre forever. Its trade is made holy. The New Testament finds disciples in Tyre (Acts 21:3–6), and Jesus says Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen his works (Matthew 11:21–22).

views.H: Tyre recovered after each siege until Alexander's causeway in 332 BC; it remained a major city under the Romans. The 'seventy years' have been dated to various periods, including Assyrian rule from Esarhaddon (about 680 BC) and Babylonian rule (about 605–539 BC).
views.C: Many scholars see an original oracle on Sidon (23:1–4, 12) expanded with Tyre and the prose epilogue (23:15–18) from the Persian period. The obscure 23:13 may be a later note about the Chaldeans.
views.J: Rashi reads the seventy years of 23:15 as the years of Babylon's rule, after which Tyre was restored. The Talmud reads 'those who live in the LORD's presence' in 23:18 as students of Torah, to whom the nations' wealth will one day come (Bavli Pesahim 119a).
views.X: Christian interpreters from Jerome on read 23:18 of Tyre's conversion; Tyre became an early bishopric. The lament over the merchant city is reused in Revelation 18.
views.F: Some futurist readers expect the final fulfillment of 23:17–18 in the messianic kingdom, when the wealth of the nations comes to Jerusalem (60:5–11).

deep.h: Tyre in history and in the prophets
deep.b:
Tyre was built partly on a rocky island about 600 meters off the coast, with a settlement on the mainland facing it. Its kings, from Hiram the friend of David and Solomon on, grew rich on sea trade. Its colonies reached Cyprus, North Africa (Carthage), Sicily and Spain. Assyria under Shalmaneser V besieged it for five years, according to the historian Menander as quoted by Josephus; Sennacherib forced its king Luli to flee overseas; Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal made it a vassal. Nebuchadnezzar besieged it for thirteen years (about 585–572 BC), but Ezekiel 29:18 admits that he gained little from it. In 332 BC Alexander built a causeway to the island and took the city after seven months.

Isaiah 23, Ezekiel 26–28 and Amos 1:9–10 all announce Tyre's fall. Isaiah's is the only one that ends with Tyre's restoration and its wealth made holy. Readers who look for exact fulfillment usually point to Alexander's conquest; others note that the prophets describe the end of Tyre's pride and its trading empire rather than the end of its people, who are still there today.

echoes: 1 Kings 5:1–12; Ezekiel 26:1–28:19; Ezekiel 29:18; Amos 1:9–10; Joel 3:4–8; Zechariah 9:2–4; Matthew 11:21–22; Revelation 18:9–19

settings.to: Judah, about Tyre and Sidon; addressed rhetorically to the ships and people of Phoenicia
settings.when: Debated: Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC, or later sieges
settings.why: To show that the LORD of Armies humbles even the richest power, whose trade seemed untouchable. For Judah, tempted to admire and depend on Phoenician wealth, the oracle placed commerce under God's plan.
views: Many: the oracle reflects Sennacherib's defeat of Luli of Sidon in 701 BC.
Others: it reflects Nebuchadnezzar's siege or the Persian period.

settings.by: A prophetic voice in the Isaiah tradition
settings.to: Judah, about Tyre's future
settings.when: Probably after the fall of Tyre's power; perhaps the Persian period
settings.why: To promise that judgment is not the end: Tyre's trade will return and be given to the LORD's service. For a community rebuilding its temple with Phoenician cedar (Ezra 3:7), the word had a concrete meaning.
